definition.text: A way of building a system in which parts communicate by producing and reacting to events, usually through a message broker that publishes and delivers them asynchronously.

facts.text: An event is a data point or significant change in state, such as a car going from for sale to sold; it only announces the change and does not say what should happen next.
The publisher is unaware of who consumes an event, and the consumers are unaware of each other.
An event-driven system has three key components: producers publish events to a router, routers filter events and push them to consumers, and consumers use events to reflect changes in the system.
The style achieves loose coupling between services, which decouples producers from consumers and makes it easy to add new consumers.
Event-driven systems are highly scalable and distributed, and building on events simplifies horizontal scaling and makes systems more resilient to failure.
Challenges include guaranteed delivery, difficult error handling, and exactly-once, in-order processing of events; such systems are complex in general and inherently hard to test.
Typical uses are metadata and metrics, server and security logs, integrating heterogeneous systems, and fanout and parallel processing.
Widely used technologies for building event-driven systems include Apache Kafka, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS and Google PubSub.

definition.text: Storing the full series of actions taken on data in an append-only event store, instead of just the current state, and treating that store as the source of truth.

facts.text: Event sourcing changes the programming paradigm from persisting states to persisting events, recorded in an append-only store.
The event store acts as the system of record and can be used to materialize the domain objects.
Event sourcing uses events as state, a different approach to storing data, whereas event-driven architecture uses events to communicate between service boundaries.
Event sourcing is one of several patterns for implementing an event-driven architecture, and the two are constantly confused.

Keeping the full history gives audit trails that can enable compensating actions, data can be reconstituted from the event store after a failure, and it suits real-time reporting and high-compliance audit logs.
The costs are a need for an extremely efficient network infrastructure and a reliable way to control message formats, such as a schema registry, because different events carry different payloads.
In a microservice system, a service such as the shopping cart emits events to a Kafka broker acting as the event store, and other services consume them, each determining its own domain model.
Change data capture can feed an event stream: a connector pulls data from tables and transforms it into events, which are pushed to Kafka for other sinks to consume.

title: Event store

definition.text: A database optimized for storing events, where an entity's state at any point in its history is rebuilt by replaying its events in order.

facts.text: Events and their data are the only real facts stored; every other object is derived from them and instantiated in memory by runtime code as needed.
Objects that aggregate recorded event data are not stored but built on the fly by traversing the event history, and discarded from memory when no longer needed.
Stored events are never changed, even erroneous ones; the only way to correct one is to add a new event with the new values.
Backdated events, which take effect before earlier events, are easier to handle because only the new event is stored and the code redetermines the objects from the new facts, with no rollback.
The disadvantage is that code may need to re-instantiate all objects in memory from the events every time a service call arrives for a given dossier or policy.
One newspaper website keeps every article, image and byline in an event store and denormalizes the raw data into views fed to ElasticSearch nodes for website searches.
Apache Kafka is a distributed event store and stream-processing platform.

title: Event correction with a double timeline

definition.text: Giving every stored event a valid date and a transaction date so an error is fixed by adding a new event rather than editing the old one.

facts.text: Each event has two dates: the valid date when it became valid and the transaction date when it was entered into the database.
A correcting event carries the new values, keeps the event date of the event it corrects, and has a different transaction date.
This ensures reproducibility at every moment in time, even in the period before the correction took place.
It also allows situations that were based on erroneous events to be reproduced, if required.

definition.text: An architectural pattern that divides a system's actions into commands that change state and queries that only read it, with separate interfaces and often separate models for each.

facts.text: A command is an instruction to perform a task that changes the system and returns only success or failure, while a query requests information without changing state or causing side effects.
CQRS extends the idea of command-query separation to the level of services, with separate interfaces to send queries and to send commands.
The core principle is separating commands from queries, which play different roles, so each can be optimized as needed.
Many systems push the split into the data: read models process queries and write models process commands, usually tailored to their tasks and often held in physically separate stores.
CQRS is often combined with event sourcing: the store of events is the write model and official source of information, and the read model offers materialized, highly denormalized views.
Benefits include independent scaling of read and write workloads, easier optimization and architectural change, clear boundaries between behaviors, and no need for complex joins when querying.
Drawbacks are a more complex application design, possible message failures or duplicate messages, the challenge of eventual consistency, and more maintenance effort.

It helps when read performance must be tuned separately from write performance, when models or business rules change often, or when one subsystem's temporary failure must not affect the availability of others.
McDonald's standardizes events with an event registry that defines a standardized schema and custom SDKs that process events and handle errors.
An event gateway performs identity authentication and authorization, and utilities and tools fix events, keep the cluster healthy and perform administrative tasks.
To scale event processing, it uses a regional architecture on AWS that provides global availability.
Within a region, producers shard events by domain and each domain is processed by its own MSK cluster.
Each cluster auto-scales on MSK metrics such as CPU usage, using a workflow built on step-functions and re-assignment tasks.

definition.text: The two main ways to wire an event-driven system: a broker topology with no central coordinator, or a mediator topology with one orchestrator that controls the workflow.

facts.text: Event-driven architecture has two primary topologies, broker and mediator, and the two can be combined in a hybrid model.
In the broker topology, components broadcast events to the entire system without any orchestrator, which gives higher performance and scalability.
In the mediator topology, a central orchestrator controls the workflow of events, which gives better control and error handling.

title: Domain events and integration events

definition.text: Two kinds of event: domain events mark occurrences inside one business domain, and integration events carry changes across bounded contexts.

facts.text: Domain events signify important occurrences within a specific business domain, are restricted to a bounded context, and are vital for preserving business logic.
Domain events typically have lighter payloads containing only the information needed for processing.
Integration events communicate changes across different bounded contexts and are crucial for keeping data consistent across the entire system.
Integration events tend to have more complex payloads with additional attributes, because the needs of their potential listeners differ significantly.

notes: Opinions on event classification vary (4885c249daca). Sentences flagged FAILED VERIFICATION (45b20d0b20ad, 28e00be194d5, 9dc8f382b953) are not used.

definition.text: An event has a header describing it and a payload carrying the details of the state change, and the payload can hold either all needed data or only keys.

facts.text: An event can be made of a header and a body, also called the payload; the header may hold the event name, a time stamp and the event type.
The payload provides the details of the detected state change and should not be confused with the logic applied in reaction to the event.
Putting all necessary attributes in the payload improves speed and scalability but can cause data consistency problems from multiple systems of record, stamp coupling and bandwidth issues at scale.
Putting only keys or IDs in the payload lets consumers fetch data from sources such as databases, which minimizes bandwidth and coupling but is less scalable and slower because of the queries.
The two payload methods are ends of a spectrum rather than binary choices, so architects must size payloads to the needs of event consumers.

definition.text: Three general ways of processing events, simple, stream and complex, plus online event processing that works over distributed event logs.

facts.text: There are three general styles of event processing, simple, stream and complex, and a mature event-driven architecture often uses all three together.
In simple event processing, a notable event tied to a specific, measurable change of condition initiates downstream actions, driving the real-time flow of work and reducing lag time and cost.
In event stream processing, ordinary events such as orders or RFID transmissions are screened for notability and streamed to subscribers, driving real-time information flow and in-time decisions.
Complex event processing looks at patterns of simple and ordinary events to infer that a complex event has occurred, and then takes action.
The events may cross event types and span a long period, and their correlation may be causal, temporal or spatial.

Complex event processing needs sophisticated event interpreters, pattern definition and matching, and correlation techniques, and is commonly used to detect business anomalies, threats and opportunities.
Online event processing uses asynchronous distributed event logs to process complex events and manage persistent data, reliably composing related events across heterogeneous systems.
Online event processing allows very flexible distribution patterns with high scalability and strong consistency, but cannot guarantee upper bounds on processing time.

title: Error handling and data loss in event-driven systems

definition.text: Ways to cope with consumers that fail on an event and with events that get lost in transit between components.

facts.text: One way to handle consumer errors is a separate error-handler processor: a failing consumer asynchronously sends the erroneous event to it and moves on.
The error-handler processor tries to fix the event and sends it back to the original channel; if it fails, it sends the event to an administrator for inspection.
Events resubmitted through an error-handler processor are processed out of sequence.
Data loss occurs when a component crashes before processing an event and handing it to the next component, so the event is dropped and never reaches its destination.
To minimize data loss, persist in-transit events and dequeue them only after the next component acknowledges receipt, features known as client acknowledge mode and last participant support.
Event-driven systems are susceptible to the fallacies of distributed computing, misconceptions that can cause significant problems in development and deployment.

title: Event granularity

definition.text: Choosing how many event types to publish and how much each one says, so consumers neither drown in detail nor do needless work.

facts.text: Finding the right number of events is difficult: too many detailed events can overwhelm the system and make the event flow hard to analyze, a problem worse when rollbacks are required.
If events are overly consolidated, consumers do unnecessary processing and send unnecessary responses.
Mark Richards recommends considering the impact of each event and whether consumers need to read the payload to decide their actions.
In a compliance check, publishing only compliant and non-compliant events can suffice, so each event is processed only by relevant consumers and unnecessary workload falls.

definition.text: Techniques for changing the shape of events over time without breaking the services that produce and consume them.

facts.text: Event evolution is hard because schemas can become inconsistent across services and compatibility must hold during gradual system updates.
Strategies include versioning events, such as semantic versioning or schema evolution, to maintain backward and forward compatibility.
Adapters can translate events between old and new formats, ensuring consistent processing across components.
Event-driven systems are loosely coupled in space, time and synchronization, yet remain tightly coupled through subscriptions and patterns to the semantics of the event schema and values.

definition.text: The four logical layers an event passes through: producer, channel, processing engine and downstream activity.

facts.text: An event-driven architecture may be built on four logical layers: the event producer, the event channel, the event processing engine and downstream event-driven activity.

The producer senses a fact and represents it as an event message, and converting data from sources as diverse as email clients, e-commerce systems and sensors to one standard form is a significant task.

An event channel carries events from the producer to the processing engine, for example over a TCP/IP connection; several can be open at once and are read asynchronously, with events queued for later processing.

The processing engine identifies an event and selects and executes the reaction, such as ordering a product and notifying personnel when stock is low, and the downstream layer shows the consequences, such as an email.

definition.text: A way to get a synchronous answer from an event-driven system by pairing each request event with a reply, using queues.

facts.text: Synchronous transactions in an event-driven architecture can be built on the request-response paradigm, implemented in two ways.
One way is two separate queues, one for requests and one for replies, and the event producer must wait until it receives the response.
The other way is one dedicated ephemeral queue for each request.

title: Timeout antipattern

definition.text: The difficulty of choosing timeout values in distributed systems, where both short and long timeouts cause trouble.

facts.text: The timeout antipattern describes the challenges of setting timeout values in distributed systems.
Short timeouts may fail legitimate requests prematurely and lead to complex workarounds, while long timeouts give slow error responses and a poor user experience.
The circuit breaker pattern can address this by monitoring service health through heartbeats, synthetic transactions or real-time usage monitoring, enabling faster failure detection.

definition.text: Domain-driven design is a software design approach that models software to match a domain according to input from the domain's experts.

facts.text: Under domain-driven design the structure and language of the code, such as class and method names, should match the business domain; a loan system might have loan applications, customers, and methods like accept offer.

A ubiquitous language shared by domain experts, users and developers is used in the domain model and in describing requirements; it is a pillar of the approach alongside strategic and tactical design.

The approach rejects a single unified model and divides a large system into bounded contexts, each with its own model; context mapping patterns such as shared kernel, customer/supplier and anticorruption layer define how contexts relate.
An entity is defined by its identity, a value object is immutable with no conceptual identity, and a domain event is an event the domain experts care about.
An aggregate binds objects under a root entity: outside objects may reference only the root, which checks the consistency of changes; repositories retrieve domain objects and factories create them.

Combined with CQRS and event sourcing, aggregate roots validate and apply commands and publish events: the input is a command and the output is one or more events saved to an event store, then often published on a message broker.

Event storming is a workshop in which stakeholders, domain experts and developers map domain events, helping to discover subdomains, bounded contexts and aggregate boundaries before applying the approach.

A bounded context often maps to a microservice, ideally one to one; critics say much isolation and encapsulation is needed, and Microsoft recommends the approach only for complex domains where the model clearly helps.

title: Fallacies of distributed computing

definition.text: The fallacies of distributed computing are false assumptions that programmers new to distributed applications invariably make, listed by L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems.

facts.text: The original list begins with four false assumptions: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite and the network is secure.
It continues: topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero and the network is homogeneous.
Assuming the network is reliable yields applications with little error handling that stall or wait forever during an outage, and may fail to retry stalled operations when the network returns.
Ignoring latency and the packet loss it causes leads developers to allow unbounded traffic that drops more packets and wastes bandwidth, and ignoring bandwidth limits creates bottlenecks.
Complacency about security leaves systems blindsided by adaptive attackers; topology changes affect bandwidth and latency; multiple administrators may set conflicting policies.
The hidden costs of building and maintaining a network must be budgeted, and assuming a homogeneous network brings the same problems as the first three fallacies.

Later additions include a ninth fallacy, that the party you communicate with is trustworthy, and three from Richards and Ford: versioning is simple, compensating updates always work and observability is optional.

definition.text: Command–query separation is a principle that every method should be either a command that performs an action or a query that returns data, but not both.

facts.text: Devised by Bertrand Meyer, the principle says asking a question should not change the answer: a method returns a value only if it has no side effects.
Because queries never change state, any query can be called anywhere, such as in assertions, without fear of side effects; adherents say this makes state and state changes easier to understand.

CQRS generalises the principle to services, with separate query and command interfaces and usually separate data models; separate models raise the question of keeping them consistent, making eventual consistency likely.

It has limits: a combined method such as a stack's pop can be more convenient, and in multithreaded code a separate increment and value call leaves a race condition that a locked increment-and-return avoids.

definition.text: Avro is a row-oriented remote procedure call and data serialization framework developed within Apache's Hadoop project.

facts.text: Avro serves in Hadoop both as a serialization format for persistent data and as a wire format between Hadoop nodes and from client programs to Hadoop services.

Schemas are defined in JSON, with an optional Avro IDL syntax, and data is serialized in a compact binary format; schemas are built from primitive types and complex types such as record, enum, array, map and union.
Data can be stored with its schema, so a serialized item can be read without knowing the schema ahead of time; an object container file keeps the schema definition in its metadata.
Unlike Thrift and Protocol Buffers it needs no code-generation step when a schema changes; the binary encoding is smaller and faster, and a JSON encoding suits debugging.
